Source (EN): A company's business assets are assumed to equal its annual sales: one dollar of plant and equipment produces one dollar of sales a year. So the number that really matters is return on capital, or ROC - your profit as a percent of those assets, which is essentially your profit margin. Push it up and the stock, your salary, and your bonus all climb with it. Click Continue.

Source (EN): Your asset allocation IS the bank's strategy, and every choice trades yield against risk. From safest to riskiest: Cash equivalents (cash + T-bills) earn the least but keep the bank liquid - you must hold at least 10% as a downturn buffer. Bonds pay a steady coupon, but their value moves opposite to interest rates, so they're a bargain when rates are high. Prime mortgages are solid, low-default home loans. Consumer loans pay more but default more in a recession. Subprime mortgages pay the most and are the most dangerous: in a credit crisis like 2008 they collapse and freeze, and you cannot sell without a huge loss. Two screens guide you - Interest Rates (favor bonds when rates are high) and Economic Data (chase yield with consumer and subprime in a boom; retreat to prime, bonds, and cash when a recession looms). Click Continue.

Source (EN): Open the Banking dropdown and click Set Allocation.
